subsubtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last June 30, on the last sitting day of the session, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) got the co-operation of the Opposition to pass amendments to and extend the life of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. This was done on an urgent priority basis to help tens of thousands of farmers get lower interest rates on their bank loans. The latest information is that over 50,000 farmers are insolvent and in serious financial difficulty. This legislation could have helped them in consolidating and refinancing debts on a wide range of agricultural costs.
What has the Minister of Agriculture done to proclaim and implement the legislation, Bill C-78, since he asked for our help on an urgent basis last June? Exactly nothing! This is the same contemptuous attitude he has displayed toward the farm debt crisis since 1984. Seven months after we rushed this legislation through there has still been no action. I call on the Minister to take action and implement this legislation immediately.

subsubtopic: SITUATION IN TORONTO-AVAILABILITY OF BUILDING SITES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one reason housing prices and apartment rents in Metropolitan Toronto have sky-rocketed is because population growth has exceeded the apparent supply of land available for residential construction. However, this shortage is more
apparent than real. There is an almost hidden supply of land which could be made available for housing and, ironically, it belongs to three levels of government: municipal, provincial, and federal.
I have in mind land around the head office of none other than the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Armed Forces Base at Downsview, land devoted to the Scarborough Expressway which apparently will not be constructed, and provincially owned land around Pickering expropriated years ago for abortive airport construction.
If we increase the supply of land we can reduce the cost of housing. Surely all Governments concerned should want to initiate such an action to meet this basic human need. I therefore urge that an inventory of government land in Metro be taken and that representatives of all three levels of government confer on the most effective way of distributing it.

subtopic: OMISSION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA REPRESENTATIVE FROM FEDERAL ADVISORY PANEL
OMISSION OF BRITISH COLUMBIA REPRESENTATIVE FROM FEDERAL ADVISORY PANEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Premier Vander Zalm is angry because the Conservatives did not include a British Columbia representative on a federal advisory panel on the effects of the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal. This is a tragic oversight because many British Columbia workers and industries will be hurt by this deal. We should have had someone on the council who would speak up for our interests.
However, instead of simply blaming the Conservatives Mr. Vander Zalm should take a good part of the blame himself. He was too quick to jump on the free trade band wagon without looking at the disastrous consequences on such industries as fish processing, plywood production, and wine-making. Mr. Vander Zalm is at fault because, instead of looking after British Columbia's interests, he trusted the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), a man who has shown all Canadians that he cannot be trusted.

January 20, 1988

subsubtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF PROCLAMATION OF UKRAINIAN INDEPENDENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Friday marks the seventieth anniversary of the proclamation of Ukrainian independence. In 1918, following the fall of the Tsarist Empire, the Ukrainian Parliament proclaimed an Independent National Democratic Republic, and based that democracy on the revered freedoms of speech, press, religion, assembly, association, and human rights.
It was a short-lived democracy as four years later a Russian communist regime conquered the independent state. But the spirit of that freedom has lived on in every Canadian of Ukrainian descent.
1988 also marks the millennium of the introduction of Christianity to Ukraine. It was King Volodymyr, later St. Volodymyr, who, 1,000 years ago, converted his people after learning of the splendid services being offered by the Church of St. Sophia in Istanbul. Upon receiving baptism from the Patriarch of that city he began building the first of Kiev's great churches, the Church of the Tithe.
1988 is an important year for Ukrainians all over the world-the millennium of the introduction of Christianity and the seventieth anniversary of the proclamation of an independent Ukraine.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF PALESTINIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they live under occupation, they have no recognized homeland, they have no passport, no freedom of movement, no vote, and little hope. They live on the most crowded piece of land on this earth. They are literal wards of the United Nations. They are the homeless Palestinian refugees.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the name "Palestinian" has become synonymous with terrorist and terrorism. This belies the tens of thousands of moderates; men, women, and children, who seek what we enjoy-peace, security, and freedom.
The children born into desolation, growing up in despair, have turned in pitiful frustration to battling a modern army with sticks and stones. Now we hear that food and clothing donated by United Nations relief agencies, Israeli Arabs and Jews, have been blocked from entering the relief centres.
Enough is enough, Mr. Speaker. It is time for this House to express its outrage and indignation.

January 20, 1988

Meanwhile we are told that the Government is getting set to produce yet another three million pamphlets that it hopes will be attractive to Canadians. Millions of taxpayers' dollars have already been wasted. I say, "Stop the presses". It is time the Government realized that all the glossy pamphlets in the world will not convince Canadians that the Prime Minister has secured a fair deal for Canada.

subsubtopic: SITUATION IN TORONTO-GRANT OF LAND MADE BY CARDINAL CARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his New Year's message, Cardinal Carter, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Toronto, said: "In our city there are many for whom there is no place. As 1987, the International Year of the Homeless comes to a close, our work has just begun".
At the same time Cardinal Carter and the Roman Catholic Church put their money where their mouth is by giving a valuable parcel of downtown Toronto land to Street Haven, a group that provides housing for needy women.
Now that all of the conferences and studies sponsored by CMHC in connection with the International Year of the Homeless have been completed, hopefully the Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will provide the same leadership demonstrated so well by Cardinal Carter.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND FIXED LINK WITH MAINLAND-CALL FOR ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the referendum on a fixed link for Prince Edward Island to the mainland, Premier Joe Ghiz has requested an immediate full scale environmental impact study of the options under consideration. However, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) called this request "the kiss of death" because it would delay the project by two years and cost several million dollars.
The Minister's credibility as the environmental conscience of the Government is badly damaged. His desire to make political hay in his home province clouds his judgment and is bad news.
Canadians are shocked. I urge the House to support Premier Ghiz in his call for a full environmental assessment. The Federal Environmental Assessment and Review Office supports Premier Ghiz and so do, I am sure, most Islanders. The environmental impact assessment is and must be given
first priority in the fixed link project. This is the only sensible way to proceed, and the Minister of the Environment should be ashamed.

subsubtopic: VAL-D'OR, QUEBEC-IMPORTANCE OF FLOW-THROUGH SHARES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 20 last year in Val d'Or, 800 people demonstrated to show their full support for flow-through shares financing of the mining exploration, after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) tabled his tax reform proposals.
Thanks to the support of Minister Savoie, the Government of Quebec has made a two-year commitment to a rate of 133 1/3 per cent.
Mayor Pelletier of Val d'Or said that just because people in the Abitibi area were unemployed, that did not make them outcasts.
Abitibi-Temiscamingue has benefited enormously from this plan, which has caused the unemployment rate to drop from 24.8 per cent in 1984 to 6.3 per cent today. What is at stake is the federal Government's commitment to a rate of 133 1/3 per cent for 1988-89. In 1987 more than $500 million was injected in mining exploration in Quebec.
So far, only Mr. Savoie, the Quebec Minister, has defended the flow-through shares plan in Canada, while our neighbour in Ontario, the provincial Minister of Mines (Mr. Conway), has failed to take any action at all.
Today, prospectors in Quebec and across Canada are in great difficulty following the tabling of the tax reform proposals and the recent stock market crash.
Mr. Speaker, I intend to continue my fight to get the Minister of Finance to revise his position.

subsubtopic: NICARAGUA-RESUMPTION OF UNITED STATES ARMS DELIVERIES TO CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It concerns the announcement in Washington about the resumption of arms deliveries to the Contras and President Reagan's decision to seek additional funding for the Contras, coming only days after the Nicaraguan Government has taken steps, its latest in a series of steps, to comply with the peace process.
Will the Minister take this opportunity to tell the House and to tell Canadian people, and for that matter to tell the international community, that Canada finds these actions by President Reagan to be jeopardizing the peace process and to be unacceptable?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: NICARAGUA-RESUMPTION OF UNITED STATES ARMS DELIVERIES TO CONTRA FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision to which the Hon. Member refers is an American decision respecting an American policy. The policy of the Government of Canada and the analysis by the Government of Canada of the situation in Central America are different.
Our view is that the elemental problems which must be addressed there are problems that are local in nature, and that the most important initiative which has been taken has been the initiative taken by the five Central American Presidents. We are, as I am sure the Hon. Member is, encouraged by the fact that the five Central American Presidents continued to make progress on the Aria's peace plan in their meeting last weekend.
The Member would know that the Presidents asked the Ambassador for Guatemala to Canada to brief officials of my Department on progress and that the five ambassadors
accredited to Canada from those countries have asked for a meeting tomorrow with me in which I look forward to discussing practical ways in which Canada can contribute to the continued movement forward of progress on the plan established by the Central American leaders themselves as to how to bring peace to that region.

Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the point. Progress is being made and one of the points that President Arias himself, who won the Noble Peace Prize for his leadership in this area, has made absolutely clear is that the United States must not do what President Reagan has announced he will do, if the peace process is to succeed.
If a country like Costa Rica, which is much more beholden and vulnerable to U.S. influence and power than presumably Canada is, can make that kind of statement, why can't the Secretary of State for once get up and say Canada is opposed to continued aid to the Contras?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an old debate. There are some who believe that the most effective way for Canada to contribute to peace in Central America is to attack the United States.
We believe, as I indicated clearly in the statement I made on my return from Central America, that that kind of preoccupation is not only fruitless but is counter-productive in terms of the influence that we may be able to have at some point along the process in encouraging compliance by all parties who must in the largest sense comply with the Central American peace plan.
There is a role for Canada to play, a constructive, substantive role. We are not sitting on the sidelines offering advice to other Governments. What we have to do is maintain intact our ability to contribute in distinctive Canadian ways to a peace process in Central America, and that is what we are doing.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF MUNICIPAL NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY CANDIDATES IN TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board.
The Ontario Government has made it illegal for supporters of political Parties to make contributions to political municipal candidates. However, now the NDP supporters in the Metropolitan Toronto area are laundering contributions to municipal candidates through the New Democratic federal Party rather than the NDP provincial Party of Ontario the way it used to be done.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF MONCTON MAINTENANCE SHOPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. The Minister is aware that CN has announced a closure of the shops in Moncton as of September 30. The foundry and rail shop components of the Moncton facility are found nowhere else in CN's entire railway system. Thus, when the shops close, some of that work will have to be done somewhere else and will have to be contracted out. In addition, CN will have to increase its staff at its Montreal facility in order to repair Bombardier locomotives, work which has traditionally been done at the Moncton shop.
In light of the fact that some workers could be rehired in Moncton to do this work and maintain some components of the Moncton shops, will the Government for once show some concern? Will this Minister intervene, at least at this moment, to save the remaining 350 jobs?

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCED CLOSURE OF MONCTON MAINTENANCE SHOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, CN is a Crown Corporation that is, of course, competing with the private sector. The assurance we can give is, that if the company is competitive, employees will keep their jobs. The reliability of CN employees and the quality of their work are guarantees for a successful future.

It is a fact that if the Minister were prepared to intervene and instruct CN to maintain some components of the Moncton shops-I am thinking of the foundry and the rail shop-350 jobs could be saved.
How can people in New Brunswick be expected to believe this Government is sincere in its efforts to promote regional development, when it has consistently refused to take action to save the 350 jobs that could be saved in the Moncton area?

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SHIPYARDS SHARE OF WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question to the right honourable Prime Minister refers to the Quebec shipyards.
The House will remember that not so long ago, the Federal Government asked the Quebec Government to purchase the Lauzon and Vickers shipbuilding yards. In a letter, the former had promised the latter to be very generous and to lavishly award contracts to the Quebec shipyards.
Yesterday, the Prime Minister stated on television that the Quebec shipyards are doing fine and that they would get their share of the $950 million contracts still to be awarded.
The Prime Minister will certainly agree that Quebecers are sick and tired of promises that do not materialize. Could the Prime Minister spell out what percentage of these $950 million contracts still to be awarded will go to Quebec shipyards? Could the Prime Minister indicate whether it will be 50 per cent, 60 per cent, 10 per cent or 20 per cent? We want a clear answer and a firm commitment!

subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPROPRIETY IN USE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Earlier today in Question Period the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) made what I believe is a very serious allegation by suggesting that Members of the New Democratic Party were using the Income Tax Act and the Elections Act with impropriety.
The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) has done the House a real service by indicating that there were no improprieties in this case, that no rules or laws were broken. In fact, the Income Tax Act and the Elections Act make this
practice not an illegal practice and an acceptable one under the circumstances.
I would like to ask that the Hon. Member for York East do the honourable thing. I suggest that he was not attempting to suggest that illegal activities were taking place, but the term "laundering money" certainly has a very clear implication in our culture and society that when groups are laundering money they are doing something illegal, something that is certainly wrong.
I suggest that the Hon. Member for York East may have something to say, that he would retract any suggestion that any impropriety was being conducted.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPROPRIETY IN USE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was certainly not my intention, nor will it ever be, to make an unparliamentary remark in this House.
My understanding of a question of privilege is that it must apply to an individual Member of this House as distinct from an entire group or Party. Therefore, I submit that this is not a question of privilege.
It may very well be that the term that was used has a variety of meanings and I certainly do not want to suggest for a moment that it is definitely illegal. It certainly was not the intention of the legislation to allow this sort of thing. I am sure that the Hon. Member would agree with that.
However, Mr. Speaker, if you feel that this is an unparliamentary remark and that this is a legitimate question of privilege, I am certainly quite willing to withdraw the remark.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPROPRIETY IN USE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I respect the views of the Hon. Member which he has made known. He has indicated that if this remark is considered to be unparliamentary he is indeed prepared to withdraw the remark.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that when members of a political Party are accused of laundering political contributions, when in fact that is not taking place as the Deputy Prime Minister so adequately pointed out, the honourable thing for the Member of Parliament for York East to do would be simply to withdraw that suggestion and allegation to clear the air once and for all.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPROPRIETY IN USE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a search of Beauchesne's has indicated to me that this is not an unparliamentary term. However, if you feel in your judgment, Sir, that it is an unparliamentary term; if you feel in your judgment that this is a legitimate question of privilege, then I will certainly accede to your desire.

January 20, 1988

that privilege, strictly speaking, has to apply to an individual, not to a corporation or a Party.
Technically the Hon. Member has an arguable point. However, one of the reasons certain things are not permitted is that if they were permitted they would create disorder or a difficulty in the Chamber. In this particular case it would appear that the reply of the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) in itself might have been adequate to assuage the feelings of any other Hon. Member. However, the Hon. House Leader for the New Democratic Party has raised this complaint.
The Chair might suggest that under the circumstances the Hon. Member for York East might rise and indicate, if in any way he was implying dishonesty or illegal activity on behalf of a member of the New Democratic Party, that it would be withdrawn.
The Hon. Member for York East takes an interesting approach. He has stated that if I find that what he said was unparliamentary he will withdraw it. The Chair is always reluctant to find anything more unparliamentary than it already has to deal with. The suggestion of the Chair is that under the circumstances, without any particular ruling on my part, the Hon. Member for York East would want to indicate that he was not implying something dishonest or illegal in the strictest term against any member of the New Democratic Party. I call upon the Member for York East to assist the Chair.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED IMPROPRIETY IN USE OF CANADA ELECTIONS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that my friends in the NDP would like me to resign at this stages.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to pursue this. We are beginning a new year, 1988. This is the first week that Parliament is sitting in the new year. I find it difficult when an Hon. Member, in this case the Hon. Member for York East, stands in his place and suggests that members of the New Democratic Party were laundering money when such was not the case. The Deputy Prime Minister said that such was not the case. There is no question that it cast a certain pall over Members of my Party and Members of the House of Commons.

speechtext:

Madam Speaker, the three petitions I am tabling today were signed by ninety-nine residents of Vankleek Hill, Ottawa, Ontario, but the majority of the undersigned are residents of my riding, Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic in Montreal. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, January 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-103, an Act to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will resume the remarks that I began a day ago with regard to Bill C-103, an Act to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
What we see before us is a Bill that takes control over regional development programs that are now in the Atlantic region, namely, the Industrial and Regional Development Program, IRDP; the Atlantic Enterprise Program, AEP; the Small Business Loans Act as it relates to the Atlantic region; the ERDA subagreements; and the Atlantic Supplier Development Program.
What we have here was presented with some fanfare. It was described as a $1 billion program. We found out that it was $1.05 billion spread over five years. In reality what we are talking about is some $200 million per year. This is fairly familiar to Members of the House who have been watching this sort of sleight of hand with numbers, which has become a hallmark of this administration, particularly over the last few years.
Since 1984, from which date we do our analysis, it has been estimated that assistance to the Atlantic area by the Conservative Government has been cut by something approaching $1.5 billion annually from various federal Government spending programs as they once applied to the Atlantic region. These $1.5 billion annual reductions in expenditures over three and a half years are scarcely compensated for by something in the order of $200 million per annum in their place. So the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency comes to its task with greatly reduced funding and much reduced ability to address the particular regional development problems of that area.
I wish to review some of that decline in the commitment in the last three and a half years. To be fair, some of that decline was in place even before the present Government took over. The fading years of the Liberal administration saw some backing away from economic development into the Atlantic region as well.
Over the past 25 years less than 3 per cent of total federal economic expenditures have been applied to the concept of regional development. Exclusive regional development expenditures in 1984-1985 for all of the Atlantic region were in the order of $230 million. To put that into perspective, it amounts to approximately 15 per cent of the amount put into unemployment insurance payments for that area.
In the five year period between 1969 and 1974, inclusive, expenditures under the DRIE industrial incentive programs have decreased in real terms. In 1969-1970 they amounted to $9 per person which declined to $4 per person in the 19841986 period. Over time one can see the backing away of federal assistance to the Atlantic region that has taken place in Canada.
In looking at specific areas in Atlantic Canada, the decrease from $9 to $4 on a per capita basis was even more sharply in decline for the Province of Newfoundland where the reduction for that same period of time was from $9 per person down to $3 per person. The commitment to regional development programs, regional development funds from the rest of Canada
to Newfoundland has been even less enthusiastic than for the Atlantic region.
During the same period of time in Ontario the amount of regional expansion funding was $10 per person, as opposed to $9 per person in Atlantic Canada. That dropped to $4 per person, as opposed to $3 per person for Newfoundland.
The disparities that the programs that have been put into place were attempting to take care of and ameliorate have in fact not changed greatly. In fact, it appears that a lot of the development programming and development funding has accrued to the more developed parts of the country at a rate that is equal to or exceeds the rate that is applied to Atlantic Canada which, by most of the indicators that we have to judge these things, is the least developed and the most in need of development funds.
The role and the assessment of regional development took place as a federal-provincial task force which published its report in May, 1987. The task force focused on five main areas where it thought that direct regional development policy ought to be centred in the next decade. It stated that the key elements of the agenda are highlighted if one focuses on those five main areas. Number one was to design the transfer system in ways that encouraged productive employment supported by income security measures.
There they are telling us that the types of employment encouragement that occurs under these types of programs should be fairly long term employment to the point where they support themselves and are not simply short term designed to employ people for a short period in the summer months and then make them eligible for unemployment assistance during the winter. This is sometimes considered to be job creation and leaves the impression that there has been more real activity achieved by these development programs than in fact actually happens.
In number two the task force is recommending that there should be a reorientation of education and training systems as a key component of public investment in regional economic development. Throughout the debate on this particular Bill we have been hearing that the Atlantic area does have many long term, long established well-known traditional educational institutions. It has very well established university and postsecondary institutions. Yet a great many of the graduates from these institutions have difficulty remaining in the Atlantic area. This is particularly true of the Cape Breton region. A great many expatriates find their way to central Canada in order to make use of their education and training.
In number three the task force reported that there should be a diffusion of innovation and technology as a prerequisite for structural improvement of the less advantaged regions. I have listened to the debate with great care and I have noted that a number of speakers have pointed out that this initiative in Bill C-103 ignores the need for infrastructure. This third recommendation of the task force is attempting to point out that there does have to be certain prerequisites in an area in order
January 20, 1988

that industrial development can take place. It is necessary to establish certain basic services in order that an industry or a region can take off.
As the agricultural critic I am concerned when I see certain parts of the maritime provinces in Atlantic Canada where Agriculture Canada does not appear to be encouraging the type of commitment to research and development that we have come to expect from Agriculture Canada.
For instance, in the Kentville area of the Annapolis Valley over time, and not willy-nilly but very deliberately, we have developed a poultry industry. It is an area that has become a centre of excellence for development in the poultry area. There are several large feed companies and some research going on with regard to feeds. There is an Agriculture Canada research centre which is doing research on a great many things, but it is one of the better institutions for poultry research. It has perhaps done more poultry research than the two other main research centres that are doing poultry research in this country. It has been particularly useful to the region where hatcheries, broiler production, processing, veterinary services, distribution and processing, research into the development of new ways of processing poultry, and handling new ways of feeding and housing poultry have all been going on for some time. It is largely based around the college at Kentville and the Agriculture Canada research centre.
On June 11, 1985 one of the poultry barns at the research centre burned down. It is now January, 1988 and that barn has still not been replaced by Agriculture Canada. There were three, but the loss of that one unit reduced the research capabilities of that station by almost 40 per cent.
Poultry research has to go through cycles. There has to be a certain amount of product going through when doing genetic, disease, and nutritional research. When one barn disappeared it took 40 pens out of the research project. It meant that approximately 40 per cent of the program had to be cut back.
Agriculture Canada does not have a system of insurance for its facilities. It engages in what it calls reinsurance, which I think is a wise business decision. It does not pay out a lot on insurance premiums. When it loses a building or some equipment, it is simply replaced out of its budget.
The problem was that the estimated replacement cost of the building was in the neighbourhood of $350,000 to $400,000. We were told that in the House in answer to a written question on December 17, 1985. It was said at that time that the estimated cost of replacement would be about $400,000. As to who would build the barn, on what date it would be completed, and whether it would be the same size as the previous barn, that information was still not known a year and a half after the fire.
A further two years went by and on January 19, 1987, just over a year ago, I again asked whether there was a project to
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
replace the poultry barn at the Kentville, Nova Scotia Agriculture Research Centre; what was the status of the replacement; what amount had been budgeted; and what time it would be completed. Agriculture Canada's response was that it did not have a project to replace that poultry barn and that it was consulting. The Government is great at consulting; it does a lot of consulting. Agriculture Canada went on to say that the question of construction had not yet been decided. As to what amount would be budgeted, Agriculture Canada said that it was unknown at that time. As to when it would be completed, it said that that was also unknown at that time.
I raised a question with the Deputy Minister last spring. I asked him what good reinsurance was if lost buildings were never replaced, and what assurance did Atlantic Canada have that this particular centre of excellence would be brought back up to steam. He said that he would investigate, and I have since found out that there is an estimate of some $250,000 toward replacement of the barn.
Perhaps, if the research station could do the building itself, it could be replaced for that amount. However, if it follows the normal procedures it is required to follow, of having it put out to tender and using architectural services, the cost of the building would be somewhere in the area of $400,000.
I only raise this matter because the Government, which claims to be helping economic development in the Atlantic region, has sat on a particular project and has done nothing with it for almost four years. The research being done out of that station is very important. For instance, it does research of a very practical kind. One example would be long-term testing to see whether expensive feed additives are necessary to control disease in poultry, whether we have to put antibiotics into poultry feed at high costs, or whether in fact those antibiotics increase the growth and cost efficiency of poultry raising.
They appear to have found that if poultry are kept on balanced nutrition and in good, dry, and well-ventilated housing, those additives actually cost money and slow down the growth process, something which means hundreds of thousands of dollars not only to poultry producers in Atlantic Canada but to those in the rest of the country.
This kind of research is being held back because the Government refuses to give the funding which that particular part of Agriculture Canada needs in order to get the station back up to full steam.
I am very concerned when we are told that this $1 billion to be spread over five years will solve the problems of Atlantic Canada. It will actually be a massive cut-back in funds for economic development going into Atlantic Canada, and these funds will not even be aimed at assisting with research, development, and post-secondary education. These funds are being targeted through only one form of economic development. If it does not happen through business, these funds will not be any good. It is taking a unidimensional view of economic development. It is saying that there is no role for Government or community organizations to play in setting up

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
infrastructures. It is saying that there is no role for educational and research institutions to play in the development of the region. I think it is a massive mistake. It is also saying that the only way to develop the region is to supply some funds to business which will therefore result in growth in Atlantic Canada.
It has been shown by previous government initiatives in other areas that heavy reliance on business to do the job which Government must do becomes unproductive. When there was an effort to change research and development from the Government to more of an initiative of business, research and development actually shrunk by the same amount as Government got out of it. Business in this country does not pick up in these areas. I am afraid that that is what will happen in the Atlantic area, and I am not sure that that great region of the country will be able to survive the policies of this Government.
I regret that the Government persists in cutting back the amount of funding and assistance to that very important region.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member's speech. I was glad to hear that the issue of regional development in Atlantic Canada is not confined to Members from Atlantic Canada.
Would the Hon. Member care to comment on a couple of references which have been made to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency by a Minister of the Crown and by Senator Murray from the other place who is to be in charge of this agency as Minister?
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) is on record as having said that this agency is the last kick at the can for Atlantic Canada, that we have tried everything and this is the last chance for Atlantic Canada. This very phrase, "the last kick at the can", was echoed by Senator Murray when he was speaking before the Standing Committee on Regional Industrial Expansion. We should combine those comments with the references of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) when he introduced the Bill. He said that they have established a board of Atlantic Canadians, that the success of this plan was in the hands of Atlantic Canadians, and that we would have to wait four years or five years to see if it works.
As an Atlantic Canadian I find that very frightening. It seems to me that these remarks are not only a backing away but a frightful derogation of the responsibility of the central Government for the problems of Atlantic Canada and for the need for regional industrial expansion and development, particularly when the Economic Council of Canada indicates in a report that uneven regional and industrial expansion across the country is the most serious economic problem which we as a nation face.
I wonder whether the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), as a western Canadian, would care to comment on that. Does he feel some sympathy for the concern
that central Canada is washing its hands of the Atlantic region?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I had great difficulty understanding what the Minister meant when he said this was going to be the last kick at the can, or whatever the phrase was, I had this brief fleeting mental image of the Minister with a great mallet and chisel chopping through rock pushing the eastern part of the country out into the ocean, saying goodbye you are on your own. We don't want you anymore. Would the Minister, who I think comes from Atlantic Canada, perhaps be on the leading edge of the run into the ocean?
It distresses me to hear those kinds of comments from Ministers of the Government, whether this Government or previous Governments. Perhaps is distresses me more coming from a region that is not always considered to be the most wealthy part of the country. I think there has to be more sympathy from the rest of the country for regions experiencing problems, whether temporary or fairly long term.
I think the solution being offered in this Bill almost ensures that the region will fail the test. When you cut back the amount of funding going into the region, reduce the amount of assistance, it is almost certain to fail. When you have the kind of cut-backs that we have seen being applied against Atlantic Canadians, I think that Ministers are putting Atlantic Canadians to a very great test. I hope that there will be an opportunity for them to put their futures into the hands of some other group of politicians than the group on which they have been depending in the past.

Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Business and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian and Northern
Affairs)): Madam Speaker, it is a privilege to make a few comments in this House on Bill C-103, an Act to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and also to answer a few questions that were raised in this debate. I will take this opportunity to review the comments heard during the consultation process that was held throughout Atlantic Canada, with a most enthusiastic level of participation.
The new agency reflects the Canadian Government's firm commitment to tackle the problem of economic growth in Atlantic Canada. Through the creation of a climate favourable to new investments, through regional participation in decisionmaking, through the implementation of initiatives that are well adjusted to the region, the agency intends to promote economic development in Atlantic Canada and more particularly to enhance employment opportunities and the growth of earned incomes in that region.

One need only look at the Speech from the Throne to see the firm commitment the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gave to the spirit and importance of regional economic development in the regions of our country. We have distanced ourselves from
January 20, 1988

the previous Government's approach and positioned ourselves as a Government which has a fresh and exciting vision. Our approach is a bold departure from the old government practice where most of the decisions affecting Atlantic Canada were made outside the region.
The Bill creates ACOA, an integral part of this Government's commitment to building a strong, economic climate in which there will be an increased number of permanent jobs and investment opportunities, a climate in which residents will be able to expect and benefit from the prospects of longer term development of our resources and from small and medium sized businesses.
This agency's primary objective is not to make up for disparities which exist, as previous Governments addressed, but to address the root causes of these disparities. It is for this reason the Prime Minister insisted the agency take a bottom-up approach. Local input and participation is the key to success and the bottom line for this Government.
When I refer to local input, I make specific reference to why it took 18 months, in the words of the Hon. Member for Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin), to reinforce our commitment to consultation and the private sector. Before the agency was created on June 6, 1987, Dr. Donald Savoie, a prominent Acadian-an Atlantic Canadian and an expert on regional development-was specially appointed by the Prime Minister to consult with representatives from all sectors in Atlantic Canada. The result was an agency by Atlantic Canadians for Atlantic Canadians, an Atlantic Canadian product delivered where flexibility, sensitivity and political will gets things done. It wants to be a non-bureaucratic, action oriented, entrepreneurial answer to our problems. I should add that the consultations have not stopped.
Since early November, Madam Speaker, the agency has met with approximately 300 individuals during these Phase II consultation meetings. Another 12 meetings will be held over the next month, involving an additional 250 business and community leaders. Their contribution is paramount to the new generation of policy and program options for the agency. This new generation will elicit, cultivate and build on an entrepreneurial spirit in the private sector.
The agency, as you may know, has been given responsibility for all regional development programs related to Atlantic Canada. The expenditures committed to date show a considerable increase over expenditures in Atlantic Canada by the previous Government. The increase is well over 35 per cent in actual dollars.
In addition, the agency comes to us with an additional $1.05 billion over five years with which to address the needs of the region and sub regions of Atlantic Canada seriously. 1 must forcefully point out that the mood of Atlantic Canadians is not any longer that money is the answer to their problems. They had money thrown at them-they have had enough of that-
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
and poured into the region in the past with no real intent or purpose being articulated, and worse, with no understanding as to what Atlantic Canadians wanted or needed.
Let us address once and for all the facts on funding. The previous speaker spoke about funding. The statements that have been made in the House are apparently based on budget papers which showed that spending under the economic and regional development envelope in 1987-88 would amount to $11.9 billion, a decline of $2.9 billion relative to the envelope total of $14.8 billion in 1984-85. A comparison of these two numbers has been incorrectly interpreted as a lowering of the Government's concern and commitment to regional development. That is not the case, Madam Speaker. The economic and regional development envelope includes many more activities than regional development per se. It includes the expenditures of some 11 departments and their related agencies.
Where declines have taken place, they reflect completion of infrastructure investments, more effective and less intrusive policy approaches; for example, our decision to scrap the flawed National Energy Program and the successful privatization efforts, such as the sale of Canadair and de Havilland. Members will remember what the New Democrats, our socialist friends, and the Liberals were saying about these privatizations, that they would be a disaster. On the contrary, they appear to be huge successes.
An examination of the changes in the level and composition of spending clearly reflects the Government's strong commitment to assisting regions, to regional development and to economic development priorities. By contrast, expenditures and regular DRIE and related programs are up some $120 million relative to 1984-85. More generally, expenditures by all federal departments and through federal-provincial regional development agreements-GDA and ERDA-in 1987-88 will be more than double the level in 1984-85. Yet opposition Members have the gall to come in this House and go to Atlantic Canada saying we are actually spending less in Atlantic Canada. Just in ERDA in 1987-88 we will spend double the amount spent in 1984-85.
I see Members on the other side nodding. They look at the figures but they cannot see them. We do not invent those figures. These are the facts. I see the Member from Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud). I heard him speak today. He should thank us. He should think about what the level of employment was when we took over from the Liberal Government. He must be honest enough to admit that the level of unemployment in the Province of New Brunswick has been drastically reduced in the last three years. That the Liberals do not like. You do not see the Hon. Member for Westmorland- Kent going to New Brunswick telling people that we have created more jobs there in the last three years. It is a good solid record.

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
There exists in Atlantic Canada today a new entrepreneurial spirit which is seeking access to capital as opposed to handouts. Remember the Liberal way of hand-outs? I think our entrepreneurs in Atlantic Canada are seeking access to capital, not hand-outs.
Going hand in hand with that spirit is the board of ACOA which is composed of experienced business and community leaders in the Atlantic region.

All are from the Atlantic region. They represent small businesses, business groups, labour groups and provincial governments. Those spokespersons also are active in their communities and have a very good knowledge of Atlantic Canada. The board, thanks to that balanced choice of representatives from a cross-section of the economy and from various backgrounds, ensures active and expert participation in the development and implementation of new programs. The board advises and guides the Minister in any decision involving the Agency's mandate, policies and options. Its influence already is clear through the contents of the Bill now before us and the programs that soon will be announced by the Minister in charge of the agency. That board has and always will have the Minister's ear.

I was most pleased to see and hear the Elon. Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe endorse the basic principle of more autonomy and more decisions being taken in the region, as well as the principle of targeting the region to try and come to grips with regional development programs. I thank him for his strong endorsement of this government initiative.
The question of infrastructure was raised by the Hon. Member for Grand Fails-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey). Being a former cabinet Minister from the far north of Labrador, I am sure he has great passion for a commitment to the brick and mortar approach. However, I submit that that is not enough.

As in any organization, priorities had to be made and the emphasis was put on activities that can have the best possible economic return for the area.
However, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Madam Speaker, would be ready to negotiate auxiliary agreements for the development of infrastructures under Economic and Regional Development Agreements, ERDA's. The funds invested in those new agreements, however, should not be taken from new funds allocated to the Agency but rather from departments with responsibility in that area, providing the provincial governments, agree on the need for such agreements.

My good friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie), is more than familiar with the details of regional development and regional disparities from the old days of DREE and DR1E. He said:
The depth of the measures open to the new agency is more extensive than
under DRIE, DREE, or other programs of the past.
This is not the superficial approach of the past. It is a flexible approach through the ACOA financing mechanism which will focus the resources of all departments of Government and all agencies as well as its own funding component on the problems in the area.
The agency does not vaguely refer to procurement, training and skill development, job creation, technology, and infrastructure development, as the Hon. Member for Grand Falls- White Bay-Labrador indicated earlier. Its mandate is to be an advocate which will keep on top of the activities of all other federal departments and agencies. It will ensure that Atlantic Canada has a voice, and I assure you that it will not be too long before federal activity in Atlantic Canada is more unified, and joint action by the departments and agencies is commonplace.

Now, the Liberal doom and gloom merchants probably want Atlantic Canadians to remain where they kept them themselves for 20 years. I am not really surprised because their position on the agency is about the same as on the Free Trade Agreement. The Liberal Party, which was viewed in the past as the party of the future, has now become the party of the past; they want to turn back the clock and keep Atlantic Canada in the past. Well, I am sorry, but this Government has decided to propel Atlantic Canada into the 21st century and to promote progress and economic development. The Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) should listen to what his cousin, Mr. McKenna, the New Brunswick Premier, has to say about the Free Trade Agreement. If the Hon. Member for Westmorland-Kent has the development of the Atlantic region and of New Brunswick at heart, he should take lessons from Frank McKenna, the New Brunswick Premier, who has not been shortcircuited by the indefensible position taken by the Leader of the Opposition in telling Atlantic Canadians: You cannot make inroads on the American market, you cannot produce in the Atlantic region, you are not qualified to do so, you are small-time and we want to keep you that way. This is not what the Government is saying to Atlantic Canadians, and the agency is a tool which will allow our businessmen, our men, women and young people to create jobs and new wealth in Atlantic Canada, to go against the American market and do business with the rest of the country. The Liberals kept us in the dark for 20 years. This Government wants to bring Atlantic Canada out of the dark, but not by imposing made-in-Ottawa solutions. Certainly not! We are asking Atlantic Canadians to be the makers of their own development, and this is the purpose of the agency!
January 20, 1988

Madam Speaker, we have heard the Members opposite say that the Free Trade Agreement was sounding the death knell of regional development policies.

1 hope the people of Atlantic Canada watch this Bill being debated in the House today. The free trade agreement allegedly prevents this Government from taking measures to ensure that we are able to fight regional disparity in the country. Yet the agreement has been signed by the Prime Minister and President Reagan and we are now introducing a Bill in the House to do just that, to equip Atlantic Canada with the tools of regional development. That is a unique approach. The people of Atlantic Canada will realize today that les prophetes de malheur in the Opposition were not telling the truth in Atlantic Canada when they told them that the free trade agreement would preclude regional development initiatives. Quite the contrary. This free trade agreement, coupled with the agencies, coupled with the entrepreneurial spirit of Atlantic Canada, will make that region a different place in the not too distant future.
I hope that Liberal Members of Parliament from Atlantic Canada, the very few from New Brunswick-one too many maybe-will put the best interests of Atlantic Canada ahead of their little political vision in the little federal Liberal Party. This represents the future of Atlantic Canada.
1 was not in the House for all of the speeches but I looked at pome of them and it is incredible that people would stand up and say some of the things they said. For example, the Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), in speaking to the House about the Bill, was talking about the question of funding. He said that we had cut $3 billion from regional development. I made the case earlier that this is totally, palpably, and blatantly false. We are spending more in Atlantic Canada.
When I hear the Liberals and NDP talking about economic development in Atlantic Canada only in terms of money, it tells me and Atlantic Canadians that theirs is the same old solution-throw money at the problem. They think that money solves everything. It has not in the past. We would rather rely on the industry of our people, on their talent and their entrepreneurial spirit. With that recipe and this Bill we shall succeed. I encourage all Members to support this Bill and vote in favour of its adoption.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what the Minister has said is unmitigated nonsense. I have never heard the facts about Atlantic Canada so distorted or warped.
Certainly we could never accuse the present Government of throwing money at the problem because it has been taking money from Atlantic Canada. The Government attempts to suggest to Atlantic Canadians that it is improving their dignity by taking money from them since they do not really want this federal government money. It even suggests Atlantic Canadians will eventually be grateful for removing this money. That is absolutely insane politics on the part of the Conservative Government.
Not only will there be reduced funding as a result of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, as compared to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, in the last three
January 20, 1988

years the Government has also whittled away assistance for Atlantic Canada.
Furthermore, there is no mention of what will happen to the ERDA funds which have been put into Atlantic Canada once those projects are completed. The Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the Senator in the other place, has stated that new money will be put into this agency. Clearly, it will not be new money because there has been no money from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion because it overspent by $900,000 in the first three months since last spring. There has been a freeze on all spending since then, including spending in Atlantic Canada. The Government is attempting to make it until the end of the fiscal year without spending any money on economically underdeveloped areas in order to impress Canadians that it can achieve a reduced deficit. However, it is maintaining a low deficit on the backs of Canadians who need assistance while giving it to those Canadians who do not need government assistance, including the wealthy, the privileged and big businesses of this country.
The Minister talked about reduced unemployment. There is no possible way to determine the real unemployment rate according to government figures. First, it will not allow its Manpower employees and counsellors to talk to unemployed people. Anyone who is unemployed will now have to go to the job board and try to obtain whatever job is available. We will be unable to ascertain from the Manpower offices exactly who is unemployed.
The only statistics we have now are from unemployment insurance cheques and perhaps some surveys. We do not know the true unemployment figure as we were able to obtain from Manpower previously.
The Government has further distorted the picture. The Government states that unemployment has come down in my area of Cape Breton. I have already stated that Manpower is unable to get an accurate figure on the unemployment situation. Second, those who are retiring and are fortunate enough to obtain a pre-retirement package are leaving without their jobs being replaced. While that represents a reduction in unemployment, those jobs are not being filled and most of our young people must leave the area.
Furthermore, there have been severe reductions in employment in our major industries in Cape Breton. Cape Breton Development Corporation has reduced hundreds of jobs. Hundreds of jobs have been reduced in the Sydney Steel Corporation and there has been the closure of our two heavy water plants and a total of 700 jobs there, in spite of the fact that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) assured us that such a closure would not take place until alternative employment was provided for those heavy water plant workers.
Those jobs were the kind of employment on which people could support families, perhaps buy a house and maybe send children to university. We have lost those jobs. In place of
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
those jobs there is part time employment at fast food outlets or department stores. There is no assurance that these jobs will continue. There are no benefits with that employment. How can one possibly build a future on jobs like that? That is what is distorting the unemployment picture in Atlantic Canada, particularly in industrial Cape Breton.
The Minister said he wanted to help Moncton. How can Moncton be helped when the Government does away with 1,200 jobs? According to the Government, this new agency is a benefit to Moncton. If so, why has it taken so long to introduce this legislation? I suggest the reason is that the Government did not want to spend the money in Atlantic Canada. The President will be living in Halifax and commuting to Moncton. That is his commitment, to stay on the job. It is ludicrous and insulting to the people of Atlantic Canada.
Not only are we losing money in regional development, the Government is decimating the whole program of assisting Atlantic Canada. Look at the programs the Government has done away with. Look at RRAP, the program which was so important in helping housing in Atlantic Canada and other parts of this country. The Government reduced the budget down to nothing. Not only that, but it made the criteria so difficult that people who need assistance are not getting it. The communities are not able to get these funds to give to people to help them improve their homes. This affects older people, unemployed people, who want to stay in their own homes but cannot possibly fix their homes up to a state where those homes will be suitable for habitation. That fund does not exist any more so those houses are falling into disrepair and eventually will be unliveable. We have not heard the worst of that crisis yet. It has only been three years since this Government has been in office and this situation is going to accumulate and worsen and the housing problem in Atlantic Canada will be a very serious problem indeed.
What about the off oil program? We were able to help people to have alternative fuels. That was done away with. What about the Canadian Home Insulation Program? That program helped people with insulation to help them save energy costs. With respect to the money that was spent by the former Liberal Government on energy, the best bang for the buck was in conservation. We were able to replace 75 billion barrels of oil a year just through conservation alone. What about Small Craft Harbours Program? Where is the budget of the Small Craft Harbours program? Ask any fishermen in Atlantic Canada and they will say it does not exist any longer. The fishermen are told that if they want to do anything they must pay for it. It is absolutely insulting.
Where is the job development program? How are we going to help our communities if we do not have a job development program for those areas which do not have the jobs? It is easy to say, "Let the private sector do it", but how are the people going to eat until the private sector does do it? What are we going to do for those people in the meantime?

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
What this Government is doing is gradually whittling away the programs and assistance that were in place. I am not saying that we should just throw money away. That is not what I am saying at all. I would like to say that I feel this program is going to work. 1 hope, in spite of all that my common sense tells me, that it does work, but I am very leary and concerned that what I see does not indicate to me that this program is going to work. There is no commitment from this Government. The evidence is everywhere that there is no commitment from this Government.
In Cape Breton, for instance, we have the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, which is an agency that has been trying to replace jobs in that area which are so badly needed. The board of Enterprise Cape Breton has from time to time passed resolutions whereby it has approved certain companies for funding to establish industries in Cape Breton, only to have those recommendations turned down by the internal board of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion in Ottawa. We cannot say that there is something about the air in Ottawa that makes them hate people from Atlantic Canada or makes them want to turn down job opportunities for people in Cape Breton, so what can we say? We are starting another board of directors in Moncton. Will that be any different? Are we just replacing one bureaucracy with another? This is no indication that anything is going to be changed. What we have done on top of everything else is politicized the board of directors that exists with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, further deteriorating the belief of the people in Atlantic Canada that this agency really wants to do something.
The Minister responsible for this agency, the Minister in the other place, has said that this is the last kick at the can for Atlantic Canada, as if to say, "We just cannot be bothered with Atlantic Canada anymore. If they do not make it this time, it is their own fault. We are telling the people of Atlantic Canada that if it does not work, it is your fault, it is not the fault of this lovely, magnanimous, well-meaning Government". Who in Atlantic Canada is going to believe that nonsense? No one. Why is it the last kick at the can? Because the free trade agreement is going to put us into a situation where we are going to be inevitably drawn towards the United States. There is going to be an assimilation of the economy between Canada and the United States, and we are gradually going to get rid of regional development in this country. This Government is going to take it away from the people of Canada. There will be no regional assistance in Canada because the free trade agreement is not going to allow it.
The free trade agreement does not say we cannot have regional development and regional assistance, but if we do give it, it is countervailable, and that is the problem. So gradually regional development assistance is going to be whittled away by the free trade agreement.
We talked today about privatization. The Minister tells us that privatization has been most helpful for Canada. I wish Members in this House would ask the employees of Route Canada who have lost their jobs through closures. That is an
example of privatization. The company was formerly called CN Express, then it was called CN Route. This Government and Canadian National decided they were going to put the workers of CN Route into a catch-22 situation. They were going to show them, especially those people in difficult regions with economic problems, such as my region of industrial Cape Breton. So they went to the workers and told them they were going to separate CN Route from the Canadian National system, all the Canadian National companies. They were told they had the choice of becoming a CN Route employee or a CN employee.
The workers knew at that time that this was a catch 22 situation and it was the beginning of the end for CN Route in Atlantic Canada, particularly in Cape Breton, but what could they do? They knew that CN Rail and the other CN companies may go on a little longer and, hopefully, go on a lot longer, but we have so many lay-offs in CN Rail and the other CN companies that there is a seniority list of people waiting to get back. If these people chose CN they would not have a job. If they stayed in CN Route they would at least have a job for what they believed would be a short period of time. That was in the fall of 1986. Sure enough, a short time later, the federal Government sold CN Route to Route Canada. The workers were told not to worry because Route Canada would protect them until June 1 and that the Government had this great package available for anyone who loses his or her job prior to June 1.
The people of Canada do not realize that the Government sold CN Route for about $23 million, and the land and rolling stock of CN Route alone is worth $80 million. That is incredible. The Government gave the new owners of CN Route a giveaway, and all that these guys had to do was to hold on to these employees until after the Government was able to launder its handling of the situation, so it thought, and the Government would then be away from the situation and any lay-offs would be the sole responsibility of the new company, Route Canada.
That is what happened. Route Canada kept the people on as a private company until after the period of qualification and assistance came to an end. Then, in November, came the layoffs in a great many parts of this area. The terminal in Sydney was closed down. Not only was the terminal in Sydney closed down but other terminals in other parts of the country were closed down as well. The man who worked there had nothing- nothing.
One of the facets of the deal was that when the transfer took place from CN Route, which was the federal Crown corporation, to the private company of Route Canada, all the employees would be starting again. But now their seniority was gone. These people started out with nothing. They are people who had worked for federal Crown corporations in Sydney for as long as 46 years. They did not even have one year of
January 20, 1988

seniority to fall back on when they were dismissed by this new private sector company.
That is the treatment that the Government is giving to people when it talks about the successes of privatization. What about the successes in terms of decency to Canadians, to people who have given the best part of their working lives to working for the country and in particular for a Crown corporation? It is disgraceful when something like this happens to any worker, but particularly disgraceful when it happens to someone who has been working for a Crown corporation such as CN Route in Sydney or CN in Moncton. There is a situation in existence here that is just not palatable to Atlantic Canadians.
1 would now like to deal with the second part of the Bill. What we have here in the second part is that the Government will do away with the Industrial Development Division of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. It will form a new company called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. This is taking into consideration that there is already an economic development agency in Cape Breton called Enterprise Cape Breton. This new entity will be called Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. There is not even any originality shown by giving it a separate name. The reason behind that is, of course, that these two will be merged together gradually and we will lose one of the two.
What is happening is that the Government is saying, "This is even better for you people in Cape Breton because it will be a separate Crown corporation". That means absolutely zilch. It is not better at all. When we had the Industrial Development Division of Devco we had, along with the coal division of Devco, a separate Crown corporation. We had a separate budget. Now we do not have that separate budget. Money will be allocated. How much will that money be? We do not know. We have no idea. No longer can we do funding for infrastructure. No longer will we be able to have a separate decisionmaking power in Cape Breton.
The President of Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation, just coincidentally, is also the President of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. So what the Government is saying to the poor souls of Cape Breton is that it is giving them something. It will give them a little part of an Act, a build up and some directors. It will let them think that they are big stuff. But when it comes right down to it, they do not get a thing. That is the way this Government is. Cape Bretoners or Atlantic Canadians-people anywhere in Canada-do not get a thing, especially if they need it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a Member from Cape Breton I disagree with much of what the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) has stated with respect to the Government's policies in regional development. When we talk about regional development it is important to acknowledge that national economic progress and national economic policies have a very significant impact on the people in the regions as well.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
For example, when we talk about lower interest rates we cannot talk about it as if the people in our regions do not benefit from lower interest rates. The people that I represent and, indeed, the people represented by the Hon. Member are paying less for their homes because they are paying less interest on the money they have borrowed to buy those homes. They are paying less for their cars. They have more purchasing power. They benefit from the lower deficit and from the lower inflation rate. They are benefiting from the lower unemployment rate.
The Hon. Member from Cape Breton-The Sydneys did not concede that the unemployment rate in Nova Scotia today is below what the national unemployment rate was when we were elected in the fall of 1984. This means that there has been substantial progress in combating unemployment in the regions. In fact, national economic growth is being shared all across Canada.
In Cape Breton, in Atlantic Canada, we have policies today of decentralization and autonomy that are bringing about substantial economic progress. In Cape Breton alone the unemployment rate in the last 12 months has dropped from 21 per cent down to around 15 per cent or 16 per cent. Our Government has committed millions of dollars to the tourism sector, the fisheries sector, the agricultural sector and the manufacturing sector. In the riding which the Hon. Member represents there has been substantial progress in terms of economic growth with relation to industries being located in his riding, particularly in manufacturing. These are industries which could not be attracted and were not attracted during the last term of the previous Government.
Those are tangible results of the economic policies of the Government. These principles are being embodied and reflected in the Bill under discussion today. The Government's economic policies have worked at the national level. In Cape Breton we have progress on the regional level. In other regions there has been substantial economic progress as well. Our record is clear. In this Bill we see the Government moving on a broader scale to put in place the mechanisms that will help Atlantic Canadians achieve greater economic progress again.
Finally, I would like to say that any suggestion that the trade agreement somehow diminishes our ability as a country to continue our regional development policies and to expand them is just not founded on fact. In fact, the trade agreement is an instrument of regional development. The Atlantic Canadian fishery strongly supports the trade agreement with the United States because it means new and better opportunities and protection for existing opportunities that we enjoy in that fishery. The forestry sector of Nova Scotia has also supported the Canada-U.S. trade agreement because we will receive substantial benefits from this agreement.
Those who stand in opposition to this trade agreement stand in opposition to a very legitimate and real opportunity for Atlantic Canadians to take a fair and equitable place in the economic structure of Canada.

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks in reply to the comments of the Elon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil). I thought that he would come to a point, but obviously there was not one to come to as far as he was concerned. He does not have much to work with when we look at the Government's program for Atlantic Canada.
The Hon. Member talked about decentralization. Let me tell the House about decentralization. There were four decentralized offices of Income Security planned for Canada in 1984 when the Conservatives took office. Three went ahead in Tory ridings. One did not. That was the one planned for Cape Breton in Sydney, a riding which happened to be represented by a Liberal. This was just the first instance of blatant Tory patronage. What did that do for Cape Breton? It cost us 85 jobs. It cancelled the training for people who were already in training, some of whom were almost finished the training for this decentralized office.
