subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, what I was saying is that it seems that the problem with the people 1 have met in Newfoundland and other parts of Atlantic Canada is that their hard work does not produce what it should because they do not control many of the resources upon which they work.
I gave the example of the timber, and I was speaking of an example of iron-the huge old iron mine at Bell Island near where my friends used to live, which was once the biggest in North America. It was owned by the British. The money, the profits, went to Britain of course. Very little stayed in Newfoundland. It is now almost a ghost town with about a tenth of the population they had there. Even of that tenth about 90 per cent are unemployed.
There is the pulpwood industry in which the profits go mostly to central Canada where we are now. There is the Iron Ore Company of Canada and the Wabash Iron Company in Labrador in which the profits go to the United States.
I do not see anything in Bill C-103 that seems likely to change any of that. In fact, it is not clear really what would be the final result, so far as building up the country goes, from Bill C-103. The immediate result is said to be giving $200 million a year for five years to Atlantic Canada. However, to take that in context, we find that that is perhaps a fifth or less than a sixth of the money that has been taken out of Atlantic Canada at an annual rate.
What we see is that during the past three and a half years some billions of dollars has been pumped out of Atlantic Canada if we consider that the previous programs of assistance were part of the funding of that area. DR1E spending cuts- they cut $200 million in 1984, $100 million in 1985-86, and $150 million in 1986-87. In the regional development envelope there has been a total reduction of $2.89 billion between 1984 and 1987, and so on.

January 20, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
It is estimated that $1 billion to $1.5 billion a year was cut off from the funding that had been provided for Atlantic Canada. In its place only $200 million is being put back. When you take that all together, it is not a help, it is a cut. It is also a fact that the control of this spending will not be in Atlantic Canada. The controllers will not be Atlantic Canadians. The board may have Atlantic Canadians on it, but we are told by Senator Lowell Murray, the Minister responsible for this project, according to The Globe and Mail in June, that final decisions will be made by him in Ottawa. I am quoting here from The Globe and Mail for June 27, 1987: "Final decisions will be made by him in Ottawa. The ultimate responsibility rests with me and a Cabinet committee made up of six federal Ministers from the Atlantic region".
So much for decentralization. It is a bit like the Bank of Montreal when it puts a branch office in your neighborhood. That does not mean that your neighbourhood gets control of the Bank of Montreal; it means the Bank of Montreals gets further control of your neighbourhood. This does not mean decentralization in the sense of giving the decision-making power in Atlantic Canada; it means giving Atlantic Canada even less decision-making power than it might have had under the previous funding arrangements.
There is another very sad and very embarrassing aspect to this, Mr. Speaker. The rate at which Atlantic Canada has received assistance has been lower in many ways in many programs than the rate at which the rest of Atlantic Canada receives assistance. The one that embarrassed me particularly is that in Newfoundland there was a reduction of the GDA/ERDA program from $126 per person down to $80 per person, while in Ontario there was an increase from $2 to $3 per person. The increase is not big in Ontario, but Ontario is getting more from this program while Atlantic Canada is getting distinctly less under the same Government.
The essence of this program is the trickle-down theory. The money is to be given only to businesses, not to a municipality. Heavens, no. A municipality might be democratically controlled, it might be controlled by the people who live there and the municipality might use it to benefit the people who live there. It cannot go to municipalities. It cannot go to municipal infrastructure, which all the cities and all the provinces of Canada have said is needed. They have offered to go shares on a program with the federal Government. The federal Government has turned them down cold. None of this money will go to providing the necessary things to keep municipalities operating. Instead, the money will go to private business people. There is no criteria, no way of identifying the principles by which it will be given to this person, that person or another business, no criteria for the performance of the businesses. There will be a review five years down the road. Of course, the importance of five years is that it is after the next election.
The trickle-down theory, which has been used by this Government and by its predecessor Government, is very simple. The argument is that we pour money in at the top and some of it stays with the people at the top, some trickles down to the people in the middle and some trickles down to the people at the bottom. It sounds fine, unless you ask, where did the Government take that money from what it poured in at the top? We find over the years, and increasingly under this Government, that tax money which the Government poured in was taken from the people at the bottom. It was taken from the working people, the working poor, even from the unemployed of Canada, while some of the biggest corporations go absolutely tax free. The corporations, many of them, are not on the list when it comes to contributing the money, but they are sure there when it comes to taking the hand-outs.
So the story is that the Government takes the money from the people at the bottom, pours it in at the top and says "You lucky stiffs. If you live long enough, some of that money we took from you will come back to you. Smile". That is the trickle-down theory on which this program is built, Mr. Speaker. To add a little further injury, they are told, of course, that free trade will solve any problems that the rest of this program does not solve. Yet the same Government that is telling them that is the Government that has opened many of our industries, not just many of our industries but many of our services in Canada-unprecedented in international trade arrangements-are now open to American competition. For example, the Department of Supply and Services, which in 1984-85 spent $406 million in Atlantic Canada and is expected to spend a little more in the coming year, will be open to American suppliers who, with greater financial resources, may be able to undercut Canadian or Atlantic bidders. It is likely that they will get even less of that money than they have got in previous years.
What this program does is not to restore control to the people of Atlantic Canada over their own natural resources and over their own labour, which they must spend on what resources are available there, what this does is to remove control further away. The ultimate decisions, according to Senator Lowell Murray, will be made in Ottawa, except for those decisions which, according to the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal, will be made in the United States.

speechtext:
My colleague asks what is left. I can tell you there is not much left for the people in Atlantic Canada. If this is the way the country is to go, there will not be many people left in Atlantic Canada.
This is not a hand-out for poor relations in Atlantic Canada. We are not asking for a hand-out for poor relations in Atlantic Canada; we are asking for justice, justice in the sense that the people who live there, the people who were born there who have chosen to settle in there, who have put their bodies, their lives and their families there, those people should have a controlling voice in the disposal of their resources, whether it is
January 20, 1988

timber, pulpwood, iron, other minerals, hydropower, tidal power or any other resource. They should have the controlling voice in the disposal of those resources, not the bureaucrats in Ottawa, not banks in New York City, but the people who live there. That is justice and that is what we are asking for.
My Party, the New Democratic Party, for example, would much rather see a Bill along the lines of what we have been advocating for over two years now. For example, we suggest a community initiative fund that would provide assistance to new co-operatives, community development corporations, small businesses and other community-based initiatives. We do not want to exclude individually privately owned businesses, and we do not want to exclude all the rest of the people, the big majority of the people, who have not been blessed with extra capital with which to be business people. We would also like to see a technological change fund to assist in private, public and co-operative ventures in high technology industries, in other words, target some of this money to where it can be viable in the modern economy. We would like to see a youth initiative fund which Canadian youth can draw on to encourage new initiatives. Again, the decision-making has to be local.
We would like to see a single industry community diversification fund to provide single industry communities with the means to explore diversification options. These towns, cities and villages in Atlantic Canada must be given back some of what belongs to them historically so that they can develop alternatives to the industries which are either exhausted because foreign entrepreneurs scooped out all the timber or scooped out all the metals, or else develop industries which would be more modern and more viable in the modern economy. As I said, there should be money for upgrading the municipal infrastructure, a thoroughly co-operative program between public representatives at all three levels of government.
Finally, there should be a decent housing program, not the kind that I saw when I was visiting Flalifax. Under the then federal Government, not the present Government, disgustingly shoddy houses were built by an entrepreneur, I am sorry to say, from Toronto. If someone is going to cheat the people of Nova Scotia, why could it not at least be a Nova Scotian? I do not really know why CMHC let him do that, but what is most embarrassing and most unjust is that those people did not even get the chance to be cheated by a fellow Nova Scotian. They were cheated by someone from central Canada.
What we need at the very least is considerable amendment of this Bill so that it will be recast in the direction of putting control of this money into the hands of the people of Atlantic Canada. That is the first thing needed. The second thing is to restore at least that level of funding, $1 billion to $1.5 billion per year, which the Government took away in the last three years. If that were done, this Bill might well be worth passing.

Its board will consist of Atlantic Canadians who will make decisions and bring forward programs in the interests of Atlantic Canadians. They will be formulated by Atlantic Canadians. The Hon. Member from Toronto spoke about the need for community initiative funds. There are such funds and they have been around for some time. There are federal-provincial agreements on technological development. There are special initiatives to involve youth. There are opportunities for singleindustry towns to diversify their economies. However, I and the people I represent know that the answer to their problems lies in the provision of long-term meaningful employment.
In that respect the record of this Government is unequalled in recent years. The people of our region are gaining improved employment opportunities, yet the NDP is against the tax credits which are bringing investment to Cape Breton, for example, and yielding better economic opportunities. They do not like the philosophy. They do not like private business which is putting people to work in Cape Breton. They are against foreign investment unless it is billions of dollars going into Oshawa. It is all right for General Motors to put billions of dollars into Oshawa but do not let the foreign corporations put money in the regions. That is not good.
The NDP are against the Canada-U.S. trade agreement, which we believe will bring improved employment opportunities to the region. It is all right to have free trade in automobiles but not fish. Keep the Maritimers poor. Do not let them sell their fish freely into the U.S. It is all right for cars to go back and forth but not fish, or Christmas trees, or pulp and paper from Atlantic Canada. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-103 concerning the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Well, we have been hearing about this agency for quite some time. It was in October 1986 that the Prime Minister announced his government's intention to take a different approach to regional development, that it would offer new programs. "A bold new approach", is the expression he used. We had not heard of it for quite some time, Madam Speaker, for you must realize that Atlantic Canadians had rejoiced following this announcement, because regional disparity is a problem which is not new in Atlantic Canada and several governments had done their utmost to try and reduce or eleminate all-together this disparity.
If some programs were successfull, others were not. But the efforts made in the past had nevertheless helped Atlantic Canadians improve their standard of living. In June, the government had announced the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. We had rejoiced again because we felt that it was finally coming. But nothing happened, except for those press releases put out by various ministers on behalf of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. But they referred only to existing programs and never mentionned the funds which would be allocated to this new agency. Yet, the
January 20, 1988

government had emphasized that it would be spending $1.5 billion over the next five years. Although it was nothing to write home about, it was nevetheless enough to establish this agency immediately, without more ado. The government had claimed that this $1.5 billion would be new money on top of funds already allocated to various development programs.
We must wonder now whether this is altogether new money. This question has already been raised by several people, agencies and organizations in Atlantic Canada. When we consider in fact this amount, we realize that it is not much. We must realize that over the years, the amounts allocated to regional development programs had been reduced from $14.9 billion to $12 billion, a difference of $2.9 billion, almost $3 billion. That is on a national scale. The Atlantic region had been affected. As you know, Madam Speaker, whenever programs are cut, we, in Atlantic Canada, are the first to feel the pinch.
It goes without saying that we support the Government's decision to establish this agency. We want it to begin its operations right away. We wish it had begun a year ago. The government has waited until the Christmas break to introduce this legislation. Why did he wait so long? That is why we question the government's sincerity when dealing with regional development.
We were promised in 1986 there would be money, there would be a new approach but now, almost two years after, we are about ready. So much so that we were told: Hurry up, this must pass post haste. Yes, post haste because of the urgency. But we must also ask ourselves how come they suddenly realized this must pass? Had they done so earlier, we could have spent last year some $125 million, the allocation for 1987. This year there would be another $200 million. Questions must therefore be raised. We are in a hurry. But on the other hand we know there probably will be elections this year. So in fact there will be over $300 million to be distributed in Atlantic Canada. Not bad. Certainly not bad. And a lot is needed.

-$200 million for this years allocation and $125 million for last year. So there will be a lot of money available this year.

Of course, Madam Speaker, you know what I am referring to. I am referring to the CN shops in Moncton. The new agency will have the mandate, a quite general one, to look for all sorts of ways to create new jobs, but also to create jobs that are there.
In 1984, there was in the CN shops in Moncton almost 1,200 workers who were earning good wages and enjoying good working conditions. But then the CN, in a rationalization effort, decided to shut down its Moncton shops.

1 am not denying that in the overall system some degree of rationalization had be done, some adjustments had to be made. But 1 what I am questionning is the need for that adjustment to be made entirely at the expense of people in New Brunswick, more specifically in the Moncton area.

At no point did a single minister feel the urge to make his voice heard in support of workers in our area.
